allEvents.label: grokLiteraryAuthor
allEvents.after:
The rustling leaves of the willow tree curled around Julian's shoulders, the air beneath them cooling as the branches took the shift. I watched the way the limbs sagged under the afternoon light and felt the same pull along my own spine. The tarot deck in my hand had grown warm against my ribs, the gold edges pressing into my skin through the linen of my shirt. I hadn't realized how much I had been holding my breath until Julian's knee knocked against mine, a low scrape of his boot sole dragged once across the etched line before he settled. A cricket began its steady chirr somewhere under the nearest root, the rhythm matching the pulse I felt in my wrist.

A faint metallic tang rose from the cards where my thumb had worn the gold leaf thinner. *Interference. The one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal.* The words settled into the hollow behind my sternum, where the weight of a dozen half-spoken bargains pooled. I flexed my fingers around the deck, the cards shifting against each other with a quiet shush. The cold press of the wood against my palm reminded me of the last time I had held the deck, of the way the cards had slipped out of my grip when the edges caught. *Petition Fate.* The thought settled into my ribs like a promise I wasn't sure I could trust. My thumb traced the edge of the card that had slipped free, the raised gold letters pressing into my skin. *Petition Fate.* As if wishing would be enough.

Julian's other hand settled onto the Alignment Circle, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. A single drop of sweat slid from his temple and vanished into the collar of his shirt before he cleared his throat. One dry leaf detached from the lowest branch and landed on the back of my wrist.

He didn't look at me. His attention stayed fixed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation. The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us, the warding gesture still poised in the air. The air between us crackled, the tension so thick it pressed against the space where my hand rested. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more. The dark brown waves swung forward as he leaned in, the long lashes lowering once to shield the sharp angles of his gaze. In the right light, it was the kind of face a camera would have loved and the room already did. The elder's voice still rang in my ears, the accusation sharp enough to cut through the hum of the gathering.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. His breath hitched for just a moment, the air thick with unspoken longing, and I felt the shift before he spoke. The way his gaze lingered on my lips before he turned his head, the hesitation in the tilt of his shoulders, the way his fingers twitched as if ready to pull away. The rustling leaves seemed to whisper against my skin, the sound carrying the weight of a decision that hadn't yet been made.

The rustling leaves of the willow tree held a held-breath stillness, the air under the branches refusing to move. I tilted my head back, letting the dappled light play across my lips, and exhaled against the curve of the deck still warm from my palm. The card beneath my thumb shifted—Petition Fate. The ink at the bottom edge glinted faintly, the edge of the card catching the light as if the paper had shifted. I didn’t pull my hand away. Not yet.

Julian’s shadow fell across my boots before I heard him. The willow branches bent where he passed, the motion arriving with him. He stood half a stride away, his stance casual but his knuckles white where they gripped the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass. The sigil under his palm pulsed once, a slow current of violet light bleeding from the lines into the soil. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on the circle, his breath measured, the count of seconds audible in the pause before he could lift his hand.

“You’re still here,” he said, voice low and deliberate. The words weren’t an accusation, but they weren’t kindness either. They landed between us as a challenge.

I wrapped my fingers around the deck, the gold edges biting into my skin. “You’re the one who hasn’t left.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, then vanished under the neutral set of his jaw. The ring clicked once against his knuckle, the sound thin against the grass. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where pressure met the lines. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs. “Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

He exhaled sharply; a dry leaf skittered across the spiralgrass between us. “Fine,” he said. “But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.” His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat.

I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s heel scraped once against the spiralgrass. The alignment-sense flared against my ribs, the pressure of it pressing against the back of my teeth, but I didn’t break the gaze. Not when the circle flared, not when the branches above answered with their own shift, not when the deck in my hand warmed like a living thing.

Petition Fate. The thought flickered through me, small and desperate. One ask. One small thing to tip the scales back in our favor.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present...

The rustling leaves of the willow tree held a held-breath stillness, the air under the branches refusing to move. I tilted my head back, letting the dappled light play across my lips, and exhaled against the curve of the deck still warm from my palm. The card beneath my thumb shifted—Petition Fate. The ink at the bottom edge glinted faintly, the edge of the card catching the light as if the paper had shifted. I didn’t pull my hand away. Not yet.

Julian’s shadow fell across my boots before I heard him. The willow branches bent where he passed, the motion arriving with him. He stood half a stride away, his stance casual but his knuckles white where they gripped the Alignment Circle etched into the spiralgrass. The sigil under his palm pulsed once, a slow current of violet light bleeding from the lines into the soil. He didn’t look at me. His gaze stayed fixed on the circle, his breath measured, the count of seconds audible in the pause before he could lift his hand.

“You’re still here,” he said, voice low and deliberate. The words weren’t an accusation, but they weren’t kindness either. They landed between us as a challenge.

I wrapped my fingers around the deck, the gold edges biting into my skin. “You’re the one who hasn’t left.”

His mouth twisted, not quite a smile. The gap between his front teeth showed for a fraction of a second, then vanished under the neutral set of his jaw. The ring clicked once against his knuckle, the sound thin against the grass. “Alignment-sense tells me the bond is fraying faster than it should. The elder claims it’s the youth’s fault. I say it’s the elder’s design.” His fingers flexed against the circle, the spiralgrass darkening where pressure met the lines. “Either way, the circle won’t last another turning without intervention.”

I shifted my weight, the tarot deck pressing harder against my ribs. “Intervention requires two hands.”

Julian’s eyes flickered toward me then, a faint scar at the corner of his left eye pulling tighter. They narrowed just enough to register the invitation. “Intervention requires trust,” he said. “And I haven’t decided you’re worth the risk.”

The air between us thickened, the willow’s rustling rising as the branches shifted overhead. My fingers twitched against the deck. I could feel the weight of the alignment issue pressing against my ribs, the elder’s life force bleeding into the earth beneath us. But it wasn’t the crisis that made my breath stutter. It was the way Julian’s gaze lingered on the curve of my throat, the way his fingers curled slightly against the circle as if holding back from reaching for me instead.

He exhaled sharply; a dry leaf skittered across the spiralgrass between us. “Fine,” he said. “But it’s your fault if the circle breaks.” His hand turned the ring again, the metal catching the light one last time before he pressed the other palm to the Alignment Circle. The sigil flared white-hot for a heartbeat, the spiralgrass hissing beneath the heat.

I didn’t look away. I couldn’t. Not when the circle pulsed again, not when the ground trembled beneath us, not when Julian’s heel scraped once against the spiralgrass. The alignment-sense flared against my ribs, the pressure of it pressing against the back of my teeth, but I didn’t break the gaze. Not when the circle flared, not when the branches above answered with their own shift, not when the deck in my hand warmed like a living thing.

Petition Fate. The thought flickered through me, small and desperate. One ask. One small thing to tip the scales back in our favor.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack. "Tempt Fate." Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present...

The rustling leaves of the willow tree curled around Julian's shoulders, the air beneath them cooling as the branches took the shift. I watched the way the limbs sagged under the afternoon light and felt the same pull along my own spine. The tarot deck in my hand had grown warm against my ribs, the gold edges pressing into my skin through the linen of my shirt. I hadn't realized how much I had been holding my breath until Julian's knee knocked against mine, a low scrape of his boot sole dragged once across the etched line before he settled. A cricket began its steady chirr somewhere under the nearest root, the rhythm matching the pulse I felt in my wrist.

A faint metallic tang rose from the cards where my thumb had worn the gold leaf thinner. *Interference. The one who had stepped between the youth and the elder's seal.* The words settled into the hollow behind my sternum, where the weight of a dozen half-spoken bargains pooled. I flexed my fingers around the deck, the cards shifting against each other with a quiet shush. The cold press of the wood against my palm reminded me of the last time I had held the deck, of the way the cards had slipped out of my grip when the edges caught. *Petition Fate.* The thought settled into my ribs like a promise I wasn't sure I could trust. My thumb traced the edge of the card that had slipped free, the raised gold letters pressing into my skin. *Petition Fate.* As if wishing would be enough.

Julian's other hand settled onto the Alignment Circle, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. A single drop of sweat slid from his temple and vanished into the collar of his shirt before he cleared his throat. One dry leaf detached from the lowest branch and landed on the back of my wrist.

He didn't look at me. His attention stayed fixed on the circle, the weight of what he was choosing to measure settling between us like another unspoken accusation. The elder's shadow lengthened across both of us, the warding gesture still poised in the air. The air between us crackled, the tension so thick it pressed against the space where my hand rested. My heel pressed harder into the spiralgrass, the blades yielding only enough to show the pressure and no more. The dark brown waves swung forward as he leaned in, the long lashes lowering once to shield the sharp angles of his gaze. In the right light, it was the kind of face a camera would have loved and the room already did. The elder's voice still rang in my ears, the accusation sharp enough to cut through the hum of the gathering.

Julian's fingers spread across the etched lines, the contact deliberate and measured, as though the circle itself might resist him. The spiralgrass beneath his palm darkened another shade, the crimson fading into a dull, resisting brown. The change was subtle, almost imperceptible, but it sent a ripple through the gathering, a collective inhale that I felt in the air thickening between us. His breath hitched for just a moment, the air thick with unspoken longing, and I felt the shift before he spoke. The way his gaze lingered on my lips before he turned his head, the hesitation in the tilt of his shoulders, the way his fingers twitched as if ready to pull away. The rustling leaves seemed to whisper against my skin, the sound carrying the weight of a decision that hadn't yet been made.
